# New renderings — odyssey-018 (4.435–537)

New house renderings introduced in this part, for copying into `conventions.md`'s table on
publication.

| Greek | `l` | `i` | avoided on purpose |
|---|---|---|---|
| ὁ γέρων (bare, of Proteus, 450, 455, 460) | "the old man" | "the old man" | inventing a new epithet; kept to the same plain rendering already established for Nestor's bare γέρων/γεραιός (row 264 of the table), since both are simply "the old man" once the fuller epithet has introduced the figure (Proteus's own fuller epithets, γέρων ἅλιος νημερτής etc., were already fixed in odyssey-017) |
| τετληότι θυμῷ (447, 459 — the same phrase repeated verbatim) | "with enduring heart" | "with enduring hearts" | varying the wording between the two occurrences; kept identical both times as a recurring formula requires, though the referent (the four disguised men) is plural and the Greek dative is grammatically singular, distributive |
| δολίης/δολίην ... τέχνης/τέχνην (455, of Proteus's shape-shifting; 529, of Aegisthus's murder-plot) | "guileful device" | "guileful device" ("his guileful device" / "a guileful device of his own") | keeping them apart as two unrelated phrases; the same collocation, δόλιος + τέχνη, is used by Homer of both the Old Man's shape-changing and Aegisthus's plot in the same speech, and the identical English is kept for both so the reader can hear the deliberate parallel Proteus's own narrative draws between his own guile and Aegisthus's |
| Γυρῇσιν / Γυραίην (πέτρην) (500, 507 — "the Gyraean rocks"/"the Gyraean rock") | "the Gyraean rocks" / "the Gyraean rock" | same | resolving the place to a modern identification (e.g. "the rocks of Tenos", "of Mykonos"); the location of Γυραί was already disputed in antiquity and remains unidentified, so the name is kept as a transliterated proper name and flagged as disputed in the note |
| μέγ’ ἀάσθη (503, 509 — the same words repeated verbatim, of Ajax's fatal boast) | "greatly blinded" | "a great blindness of mind" | "was greatly deluded", "was struck mad", "acted with great folly" (all lose the specific ἀάομαι root, the same one behind the goddess Ἄτη); kept identical in both occurrences since the poet's repetition marks the same reckless moment referred to twice |
| δολιχηρέτμοισι (of the ships bearing Ajax's fleet, 499) | "long-oared" | "long-oared" | "long-benched" (confuses ἐρετμόν "oar" with a rowing-bench), "well-oared" |
| ἁλιοτρεφέων (442, of the seals) | "sea-bred" | "sea-bred" | flagging as unknown; the compound (ἅλς + τρέφω) is transparent even though otherwise unattested, so it is translated plainly rather than marked disputed |
| ζατρεφέας (451, of the seals) | "sleek" | "well-fed" | flagging as unknown; ζα- is the familiar intensive prefix (= δια-) on τρέφω "nourish", so "well-fed, sleek" follows directly from the formation |
| ὣς ἐφάμην, ὁ δέ μ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπεν· (a new reply-formula, first at 471, recurring verbatim at 491) | "So I spoke, and he then at once, answering me, addressed me:" | "So I said, and he answered me at once:" | using the gender-neutral formula already fixed at 4.464 ("So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:"); ὁ here is explicitly masculine and the situation (Menelaus reporting Proteus's reply) is the mirror image of that one, so a distinct formula is fixed for it, to be kept identical at every future recurrence |

## Judgment calls not producing a new table row

- **Quotation-mark scheme.** Proteus's three speeches within this part (462–463, 472–480, 492–…)
  each open with a fresh “ ” pair, on his own, distinct-character footing (paralleling Eidothea's
  role in odyssey-017), while Menelaus's own recalled replies (465–470, 485–490) open and close with
  a single ‘ ’ pair, nested inside his still-open outer narration begun at 4.333. Proteus's third
  speech (492 onward) is left open at the part's end, since the Agamemnon story runs on past line 537
  in the poem.
- **ποιμένι/ποιμένα λαῶν (528, 532).** Both occurrences of the already-fixed "shepherd of the
  people" are kept to that exact wording; the note at 528 clarifies that this occurrence names
  Aegisthus, in his usurped position as local master, not Agamemnon.
- **ἀεικέα μερμηρίζων (533).** ἀεικής is kept to its already-fixed sense "unseemly" (as in ἀεικέα
  πότμον), even though the noun πότμον is absent here and the adjective stands alone, substantively,
  as the object of μερμηρίζων.
